title: Working conditions, security and grievance management among Bundibugyo virus response personnel: exploratory findings from an anonymous survey in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo

analysis.scope_and_question: Of 55 submissions, 54 respondents consented and were analysed; denominators fall further, to 21, for grievance items because of within-survey drop-off.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: Approach We conducted an anonymous, self-administered online survey in French among BVD response personnel in North Kivu, Ituri and South Kivu, covering staffing, EPI supply, remuneration, security incidents, grievances and psychosocial well-being.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: 67% reported a security incident in three months; among the smaller subgroup reaching the grievance questions, 57% feared reprisal.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: In eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, repeated Ebola-family outbreaks have occurred alongside armed conflict and institutional distrust [1], but working conditions, security exposure and grievance handling among response personnel are rarely documented systematically during an active response.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: Working conditions, security and grievance management should be monitored as core infection-prevention-and-control and occupational-risk indicators, not as a peripheral human-resources matter.

analysis.summary_en: Of 55 submissions, 54 respondents consented and were analysed; denominators fall further, to 21, for grievance items because of within-survey drop-off. Approach We conducted an anonymous, self-administered online survey in French among BVD response personnel in North Kivu, Ituri and South Kivu, covering staffing, EPI supply, remuneration, security incidents, grievances and psychosocial well-being. 67% reported a security incident in three months; among the smaller subgroup reaching the grievance questions, 57% feared reprisal. In eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, repeated Ebola-family outbreaks have occurred alongside armed conflict and institutional distrust [1], but working conditions, security exposure and grievance handling among response personnel are rarely documented systematically during an active response. Working conditions, security and grievance management should be monitored as core infection-prevention-and-control and occupational-risk indicators, not as a peripheral human-resources matter.

title: Notes from the Field: Clinical Characteristics of Patients with Ebola Disease Caused by Bundibugyo Virus - Uganda, 2026.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to describe the clinical and epidemiological characteristics of a Bundibugyo virus (BVD) outbreak in Uganda, following an importation from the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). The outbreak was declared over with 20 confirmed cases and one probable case, highlighting the need for understanding the disease to inform surveillance and management.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A case investigation was conducted in Uganda, involving 21 cases of BVD, including one index patient who was a man from DRC. The study covered the period from May 15 to August 26, 2026, and included patients from a private hospital in Kampala.
analysis.methods: The study involved clinical case investigations, including patient interviews and medical records review. No specific laboratory or statistical methods were detailed in the provided evidence.
analysis.main_results: The study reported 20 confirmed and one probable case of BVD in Uganda. The index patient died despite supportive care. Common signs and symptoms included fever, abdominal pain, diarrhea, vomiting, weakness, and bleeding. Case-fatality rates among confirmed cases were not explicitly stated.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted the findings to describe the clinical and epidemiological characteristics of BVD, contributing to the understanding of the disease in Uganda. The study highlighted the importance of early detection and supportive care.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings can inform surveillance and management strategies for BVD, particularly in regions where the virus is endemic or where importations occur. The study underscores the need for continued vigilance and preparedness.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by the small sample size and the fact that it only covered one outbreak. The lack of specific laboratory or statistical methods reduces the strength of the evidence.

analysis.summary_en: This study described the clinical and epidemiological characteristics of a Bundibugyo virus outbreak in Uganda, highlighting the importance of early detection and supportive care. The findings contribute to understanding the disease and inform surveillance and management strategies.

title: Notes from the Field: Characteristics and Monitoring of the 2026 Outbreak of Ebola Disease Caused by Bundibugyo Virus - Democratic Republic of the Congo, August 2026.

analysis.research_question_and_background: This report addresses the characteristics and monitoring of the 2026 Ebola disease outbreak caused by Bundibugyo virus in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, highlighting the need for improved operational and surveillance mechanisms to control the outbreak.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study is a field report documenting the 2026 Ebola disease outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, focusing on the Bundibugyo virus. It spans from August 2026 and involves public health response activities in affected health zones.
analysis.methods: The methods include the expansion of community-based surveillance systems, improvements in contact tracing, laboratory testing, isolation of infected persons, and safe and dignified burials as critical response areas. Data collection at the health zone level is emphasized.
analysis.main_results: Most operational indicator measures remained below established response targets, and data for others were unavailable, indicating gaps in surveillance, contact tracing, laboratory testing, health care–seeking, isolation, and SDB capacity. The outbreak is now the second largest in history.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings indicate that the outbreak is expanding rapidly and that current operational measures are insufficient, necessitating substantial improvements in outbreak control strategies. The report adds that this is the second largest Ebola outbreak ever recorded.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The report underscores the importance of strengthening surveillance, contact tracing, and laboratory testing to effectively control the outbreak. It highlights the need for international coordination and support to address the ongoing public health crisis.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The evidence is based on operational data and public health response indicators, which may be limited by the ongoing complex humanitarian emergency. The confidence in the findings is moderate due to the reliance on available data and the challenges in data collection.

analysis.summary_en: This report details the characteristics and monitoring of the 2026 Ebola disease outbreak caused by Bundibugyo virus in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. It highlights the need for improved operational and surveillance mechanisms to control the outbreak. The study documents the ongoing public health response activities in affected health zones, emphasizing the expansion of community-based surveillance, contact tracing, and laboratory testing. The main results indicate that most operational indicators remain below established targets, and the outbreak is now the second largest in history. The authors interpret these findings as evidence of uncontrolled expansion and the necessity for substantial improvements in outbreak control measures. The report adds that the outbreak is the second largest ever recorded, underscoring the importance of strengthening surveillance and response efforts. The findings suggest that international coordination and support are critical for addressing the ongoing public health crisis. However, the evidence is limited by the challenges of data collection in a complex humanitarian emergency, resulting in a moderate confidence assessment.

title: Evidence for cross-reactivity and protection against Bundibugyo virus disease after heterologous vaccination: a systematic review and meta-analysis

analysis.scope_and_question: The available data demonstrate immune cross-reactivity and some evidence for protection in animals, although further clinical and pre-clinical data is urgently needed to inform decisions on the use of Ervebo to protect against Bundibugyo virus disease.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: We find on average a 2.8-fold (95% predictive interval, PI: 2.6-3.0) drop in binding (n = 8 observations from 4 studies) and 3.1-fold drop (95% PI: 2.0-4.8) in neutralization (n = 2 observations from 1 study) between Ebola virus and BDBV antigens after Ervebo vaccination, which appears maintained over time after vaccination.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: A single study in NHP showed non-significant vaccine protection from BDBV challenge, while a study in ferrets showed significant protection after both one and two doses.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: Very limited data on cross reactivity after Zabdeno/Mvabea vaccination suggests a higher drop in recognition of BDBV (39.7-fold, 95% PI: 24.8-63.8; n = 3 observations from 2 studies).
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: There are currently no approved vaccines or medical countermeasures for use in prevention or treatment of Bundibugyo virus disease.

analysis.summary_en: The available data demonstrate immune cross-reactivity and some evidence for protection in animals, although further clinical and pre-clinical data is urgently needed to inform decisions on the use of Ervebo to protect against Bundibugyo virus disease. We find on average a 2.8-fold (95% predictive interval, PI: 2.6-3.0) drop in binding (n = 8 observations from 4 studies) and 3.1-fold drop (95% PI: 2.0-4.8) in neutralization (n = 2 observations from 1 study) between Ebola virus and BDBV antigens after Ervebo vaccination, which appears maintained over time after vaccination. A single study in NHP showed non-significant vaccine protection from BDBV challenge, while a study in ferrets showed significant protection after both one and two doses. Very limited data on cross reactivity after Zabdeno/Mvabea vaccination suggests a higher drop in recognition of BDBV (39.7-fold, 95% PI: 24.8-63.8; n = 3 observations from 2 studies). There are currently no approved vaccines or medical countermeasures for use in prevention or treatment of Bundibugyo virus disease.

title: Detected case growth and outcome heterogeneity during the 2026 Bundibugyo virus disease outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Uganda

analysis.research_question_and_background: The 2026 Bundibugyo virus disease outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and Uganda evolved amid mobility, insecurity, delayed detection, laboratory constraints, and pressure on case management. The study aimed to assess how official aggregate data with documented source provenance could support real-time description of reported case growth, outcome heterogeneity, and response constraints.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A retrospective aggregate time-series and subnational ecological analysis was conducted using official situation reports and public health updates from the DRC and Uganda during the early 2026 Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD) outbreak.
analysis.methods: The analysis used national, provincial, and health-zone data from situation reports covering the period from 14 May to 11 June 2026 for the DRC, and separate analysis for Uganda through 10 June 2026. Outcomes included epidemic trajectory, growth of reported cumulative confirmed cases, crude observed case-fatality ratios (CFRs), and selected operational indicators.
analysis.main_results: Between 14 May and 11 June 2026, the DRC recorded 689 confirmed cases and 139 confirmed deaths across 29 health zones, corresponding to a crude observed CFR of 20.2% (95% CI 17.2–23.4%). Ituri province accounted for 646 cases (93.8%) and had a CFR of 17.6% (95% CI 14.8–20.8%). By 10 June 2026, Uganda had recorded 19 confirmed cases and two confirmed deaths. Apparent doubling times were similar during 21–27 May and 4–10 June 2026 (10.5 and 10.3 days, respectively), with a shorter estimate of 7.4 days during 28 May–3 June 2026. Among eligible Ituri health zones, CFRs ranged from 3.0% in Nyankunde to 38.2% in Mongbwalu. Contact follow-up reached 71.8% on 10 June. Ituri test positivity ranged from 26.6% to 68.5% across four reported time points.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The study found that growth estimates were treated as descriptive measures of reported case accumulation, not direct estimates of transmission intensity. The phase-specific growth estimates were sensitive to surveillance-series representation and should be interpreted primarily as descriptive measures of reported case accumulation, not direct transmission estimates.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings can inform surveillance, diagnosis, and response strategies for future BVD outbreaks. Transparent documentation of revisions, unresolved outcomes, and subnational data gaps is essential for credible real-time outbreak analysis.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by the design, which relies on official aggregate data with potential for underreporting and incomplete data. The evidence strength is moderate due to the retrospective nature and the sensitivity of growth estimates to surveillance-series representation.

analysis.summary_en: The study assessed the 2026 Bundibugyo virus disease outbreak in the DRC and Uganda, finding that reported case growth and CFRs varied significantly across health zones, with Ituri province accounting for the majority of cases and deaths. The study highlighted the importance of transparent documentation and real-time analysis for credible outbreak response.

title: Early Action Review of Detection, Notification, and Response Timeliness during Cross-Border Bundibugyo Virus Disease Outbreak, Uganda, 2026

analysis.scope_and_question: The review focuses on the detection, notification, and response timeliness during a cross-border Bundibugyo virus disease outbreak in Uganda and the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) in 2026. The central question is whether the outbreak response met the 7-1-7 framework targets for timely detection, notification, and response actions.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: The review was conducted as a 2-day workshop using the 7-1-7 framework to assess outbreak response timeliness. The evidence includes data on the outbreak timeline, case counts, case-fatality rates, and the identification of bottlenecks and enablers in the response. The review does not report on meta-analysis or pooled estimates but relies on descriptive findings from the outbreak response.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: Uganda met all three 7-1-7 targets: detection within 6 days, notification within <1 day, and response completion within 2 days. The review highlights that the cross-border nature of the outbreak was underscored by the importation of 15 cases from the DRC, and the need for sustained joint surveillance and coordinated screening along the Uganda–DRC corridor.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The review identifies low clinical suspicion, cross-border data-sharing gaps, fragmented digital systems, and delayed community engagement as common bottlenecks. It also notes that while no licensed vaccine or specific therapeutic exists for BVD, Zaire ebolavirus vaccines show partial cross-reactive immunogenicity, and BVD-specific vaccines and therapeutics are undergoing WHO-led prioritization. These findings suggest gaps in current response strategies and the need for improved coordination and community engagement.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: The review emphasizes the need for sustained joint surveillance and coordinated screening along the Uganda–DRC corridor to address cross-border data-sharing gaps and fragmented digital systems. It also highlights the importance of developing BVD-specific vaccines and therapeutics, as well as improving clinical suspicion and community engagement to enhance outbreak response effectiveness.

analysis.summary_en: This review evaluates the detection, notification, and response timeliness during a cross-border Bundibugyo virus disease outbreak in Uganda and the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) in 2026. Using the 7-1-7 framework, the review found that Uganda met all three targets: detection within 6 days, notification within <1 day, and response completion within 2 days. The outbreak involved 20 confirmed cases, with 15 directly imported from the DRC, highlighting the need for joint surveillance and coordinated screening. Key challenges included low clinical suspicion, fragmented digital systems, and delayed community engagement. The review underscores the importance of developing BVD-specific vaccines and therapeutics, as no licensed options currently exist. It also calls for improved data-sharing and response coordination across borders to prevent future outbreaks.

title: Sub-national heterogeneity in the time-varying reproduction number during the 2026 Bundibugyo virus disease outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo: a hierarchical Bayesian analysis

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to assess sub-national heterogeneity in the time-varying reproduction number (Rt) during the 2026 Bundibugyo virus disease (BDBV) outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), as national-level estimates may not capture local variations in transmission.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study conducted a hierarchical Bayesian analysis of the 2026 BDBV outbreak across five provinces in the DRC, focusing on estimating Rt at national, provincial, and health-zone levels where sufficient case data was available.
analysis.methods: The researchers used a standard sliding-window estimator and a hierarchical Bayesian renewal model with partial pooling across spatial units, fitted by Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (No-U-Turn Sampler) to account for sub-national variations in transmission.
analysis.main_results: Provincial estimates of Rt diverged from the national trend, with Ituri having a median of 0.91 (95% credible interval [CrI] 0.68 - 1.24), Nord-Kivu at 1.23 (0.87 - 1.72), and Haut-Uele at 1.79 (1.24 - 2.67). Health-zone analysis revealed further heterogeneity, with some zones showing declining transmission while others remained above the epidemic threshold.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings highlight the importance of sub-national analysis in understanding transmission dynamics, as they reveal significant local variations that a single national estimate might obscure.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These results can inform targeted public health interventions by identifying specific zones with ongoing supercritical transmission, allowing for more effective resource allocation and outbreak control strategies.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: Aggregation at higher spatial levels may mask important local heterogeneity, and reliance on case volume for health-zone analysis limits the scope of detailed sub-national insights. The evidence strength is moderate, as the study addresses these limitations through explicit model checks and sensitivity analyses.

analysis.summary_en: This study analyzed the 2026 Bundibugyo virus disease (BDBV) outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) to assess sub-national heterogeneity in the time-varying reproduction number (Rt). National-level estimates suggested convergence near the epidemic threshold, but provincial estimates revealed significant variation, with some areas still experiencing supercritical transmission. Health-zone analysis further highlighted localized differences, showing that even within provinces, transmission intensity varied. The study used a hierarchical Bayesian renewal model with partial pooling and Hamiltonian Monte Carlo to estimate Rt, addressing limitations in data reporting and model assumptions. The findings emphasize the need for localized surveillance and response strategies to effectively manage outbreaks. However, the study acknowledges that aggregation may obscure important heterogeneity, and the evidence strength is moderate due to these limitations.

title: Discovering host-viral protein interactions in autophagy: A LIR discovery pipeline for identifying LC3-interacting region motifs in highly virulent viruses.

analysis.research_question_and_background: HFVs and other highly virulent viruses (HVVs), such as Nipah virus, exploit host cell pathways, including the conserved host autophagy pathway, to promote viral replication.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The supplied evidence does not clearly state the study design, setting, or study population.
analysis.methods: To address this gap, we developed the LIR Discovery Pipeline (LIR-DP) which integrates amino acid sequence pattern matching, with protein disorder prediction using IUPred3, and modeling with AlphaFold3.
analysis.main_results: Using LIR-DP, we identified 43 putative LIR motifs in 166 proteins from 22 HVVs and predicted that 18 of these LIRs would be functional.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The aromatic amino acid in the first position of each LIR motif was found to be critical for these interactions.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: We provide evidence for the utility of the LIR-DP in identifying functional LIRs within HVV proteins which may provide valuable insight into the mechanism by which HVVs modulate the autophagy pathway during infection.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: This deterministic extraction is based on retrieved fulltext evidence. The source does not explicitly report enough limitations for an independent appraisal, so confidence is low.

analysis.summary_en: HFVs and other highly virulent viruses (HVVs), such as Nipah virus, exploit host cell pathways, including the conserved host autophagy pathway, to promote viral replication. The supplied evidence does not clearly state the study design, setting, or study population. To address this gap, we developed the LIR Discovery Pipeline (LIR-DP) which integrates amino acid sequence pattern matching, with protein disorder prediction using IUPred3, and modeling with AlphaFold3. Using LIR-DP, we identified 43 putative LIR motifs in 166 proteins from 22 HVVs and predicted that 18 of these LIRs would be functional. The aromatic amino acid in the first position of each LIR motif was found to be critical for these interactions. We provide evidence for the utility of the LIR-DP in identifying functional LIRs within HVV proteins which may provide valuable insight into the mechanism by which HVVs modulate the autophagy pathway during infection. This deterministic extraction is based on retrieved fulltext evidence. The source does not explicitly report enough limitations for an independent appraisal, so confidence is low.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Evidence on the incremental benefits of meeting these targets in resource-constrained settings remains limited.
analysis.study_design_and_population: For measles, 81 cases and one death would be averted (ICER 83 USD/DALY).
analysis.methods: Cost-effectiveness was assessed using Disability-Adjusted Life Years (DALYs) averted and Incremental Cost-Effectiveness Ratios (ICERs).
analysis.main_results: Results Under the modelled 7–1-7 scenario, 133 SVD cases (47 deaths) and 1,409 DALYs would be averted, with an ICER of −17.46 USD/DALY (cost-saving).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Conclusion The 7–1-7 framework substantially reduces cases, deaths, and costs across three diverse diseases.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: Surveillance data from recent outbreaks informed the models.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: This deterministic extraction is based on retrieved fulltext evidence. The source does not explicitly report enough limitations for an independent appraisal, so confidence is low.

analysis.summary_en: Evidence on the incremental benefits of meeting these targets in resource-constrained settings remains limited. For measles, 81 cases and one death would be averted (ICER 83 USD/DALY). Cost-effectiveness was assessed using Disability-Adjusted Life Years (DALYs) averted and Incremental Cost-Effectiveness Ratios (ICERs). Results Under the modelled 7–1-7 scenario, 133 SVD cases (47 deaths) and 1,409 DALYs would be averted, with an ICER of −17.46 USD/DALY (cost-saving). Conclusion The 7–1-7 framework substantially reduces cases, deaths, and costs across three diverse diseases. Surveillance data from recent outbreaks informed the models. This deterministic extraction is based on retrieved fulltext evidence. The source does not explicitly report enough limitations for an independent appraisal, so confidence is low.

title: MHRN Roundtable Report: Social and Behavioural Science Priorities for Ebola Clinical Trials in DRC

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to address the need for integrating social and behavioural science (SBS) and risk communication and community engagement (RCCE) into Ebola clinical trials to improve their design and implementation.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study was a roundtable discussion held on 18 August 2026 in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), bringing together SBS researchers, trial implementers, RCCE specialists, and Ebola responders.
analysis.methods: The methods involved a structured online roundtable discussion to consolidate lessons learned from past SBS research in Ebola clinical trials and to discuss current challenges with trial design and rollout.
analysis.main_results: The discussion highlighted important lessons from past outbreaks, including the impact of rumour, mistrust, participant experience, protocol changes, and the inclusion of vulnerable groups.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted these findings as demonstrating the value of integrating SBS and RCCE from the beginning of clinical trials to enhance their effectiveness and address contextual challenges.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings can inform future Ebola clinical trials by emphasizing the importance of incorporating social and behavioural insights to improve feasibility, recruitment, retention, and trust.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited to a discussion format and does not include empirical data, but the evidence is strong due to the integration of multiple expert perspectives and prior research findings.

analysis.summary_en: This report outlines the importance of integrating social and behavioural science (SBS) and risk communication and community engagement (RCCE) into Ebola clinical trials. It highlights the need for these approaches to address challenges such as mistrust, rumour, and the inclusion of vulnerable groups, based on lessons from past outbreaks in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). The study was a roundtable discussion held on 18 August 2026, involving SBS researchers, trial implementers, RCCE specialists, and Ebola responders. The findings suggest that incorporating SBS and RCCE from the outset can improve trial design and implementation. The report emphasizes the significance of these insights for future Ebola trials, particularly in enhancing feasibility and trust. However, the study is limited to a discussion format and lacks empirical data, which may affect the strength of the evidence. The confidence in the findings is moderate due to the nature of the evidence and the absence of quantitative results.

title: Optimal control metapopulation models for the West Africa Ebola epidemic and their nonstandard finite difference discretizations

analysis.research_question_and_background: The 2014-2016 Ebola Virus disease (EVD) outbreak came with an unprecedented challenge. It simultaneously arose in three different countries with considerable inbound and outbound travels, leading the World Health Organization (WHO) to suggest implementing exit screening of travelers at their borders.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This paper considers two optimal controls for patch models in which other interventions supplement exit screening.
analysis.methods: We prove the well-posedness of both optimal control problems and construct a new Nonstandard Finite Difference Forward-Backward-Sweep-Method, which preserves the dynamics of the continuous model. Numerical simulations that support the theory are provided.
analysis.main_results: The numerical simulations suggest that vaccination alone is effective in reducing the disease burden.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The paper introduces two optimal control problems for patch models and develops a new numerical method to solve them, providing insights into the effectiveness of different interventions.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings can inform the design of optimal control strategies for future outbreaks, particularly focusing on the combination of exit screening and vaccination.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is based on mathematical models and simulations, which may not fully capture the complexities of real-world scenarios. The evidence strength is moderate.

analysis.summary_en: This paper addresses the 2014-2016 Ebola outbreak by considering optimal control strategies for patch models, focusing on exit screening and vaccination. Numerical simulations suggest that vaccination alone can effectively reduce the disease burden.
